get.description:
Prometheus text exposition (format 0.0.4), only with
`PANEL_METRICS=true` - 404 otherwise. Open on the LAN like every read:
never expose the panel to the WAN.

Counters, since the panel started (a restart resets them):
`insights_device_bytes_total{device,direction}`,
`insights_group_bytes_total{group,direction}`,
`insights_exit_bytes_total{exit,direction}`,
`insights_rule_bytes_total{rule_type,direction}`,
`insights_category_bytes_total{category,direction}`,
`insights_country_bytes_total{country,direction}` - `direction` is
`up` or `down`. An empty value is written `no_dictionary` (category,
bytes counted without a dictionary) or `none` (anything else, e.g. a
flow no rule decided). Gauges mirror `/health`: `insights_collector_*`,
`insights_stats_*`, `insights_mihomo_*`. No label carries a hostname,
sniffed name, ASN, port or app-level id.

post.description:
Bulk-import aliases from ANY source. Vendor-agnostic on purpose:
`source` is just a label, so UniFi, Nimbus and a hand-written file all
use this one path and no vendor code or credential lives in the panel.

An alias an operator typed OUTRANKS every importer, so a row whose
recorded source differs is left alone. The response is therefore a
per-row LEDGER rather than a count - a skip is a designed refusal, and
the caller has to see WHICH hosts kept their typed name. Reporting only
a total would hide exactly the case the rule exists to protect.

`override: true` is the attended escape hatch, so re-pointing a renamed
host at its vendor name does not require destroying the name first.

schema.title: Response Post Identities Import V1 Identities Import Post

get.description:
Aliases for hosts that may or may not carry a routing policy - the
reason this is not folded into /v1/devices, which only ever lists
devices that HAVE one.

schema.title: Response Get Identity V1 Identity Get

delete.description:
Answers 200 with `removed: false` when there was no alias, NOT 404.
This diverges deliberately from `DELETE /v1/devices/{id}`: a device id
either names a resource or does not, whereas every valid host address
exists whether or not it carries a label, so "there was nothing to
remove" is a truthful outcome rather than a missing resource.

schema.title: Response Delete Identity V1 Identity  Ip  Delete

put.description:
Set (or clear) the alias for one host. PUT replaces the resource, so
a body carrying no alias clears it - `removed` reports whether a row
actually went away, since the cleared state is otherwise identical to
an address that never had one.

Naming a device applies no policy and triggers no reconcile: there is
nothing for the gateway to do about a label. That also means an alias
write is NOT followed by a `backup_db` the way a policy mutation is -
aliases enter a backup on the next policy change (deliberate: a bulk
import must not VACUUM per row).

`{ip}` is a single host by construction. A CIDR's `/` is a path
separator, so a range cannot address this endpoint at all.

schema.title: Response Put Identity V1 Identity  Ip  Put

get.description:
Every known setting with its effective value, the default it would
fall back to, and whether an override is in force.

Reporting all three is deliberate: an inherited value shown as if it
were a stored choice is the same class of lie as a badge that claims
an apply reached mihomo when it did not. The timezone default is the
container's own `TZ`, so an untouched panel agrees with mihomo and the
updater about what "today" means.

schema.title: Response Get Settings V1 Settings Get

put.description:
Apply a partial map of overrides. A blank value REVERTS that key to
its code default rather than storing an empty string.

The batch is all-or-nothing: every key and value is validated before
anything is written, so a typo cannot leave half a change behind. This
diverges from `POST /v1/identities/import`, whose per-row ledger is
the honest answer there because the rows are independent hosts - a
settings write is a single operator intent.

`changed` lists the keys whose stored OVERRIDE moved. That is broader
than "the resolved value moved" on purpose: pinning today's default, or
reverting a pin that equals today's default, changes nothing visible now
but changes what a later redeploy does. Re-sending an identical
configuration is still a truthful no-op.

schema.title: Response Put Settings V1 Settings Put

get.description:
One dimension's values over a window, largest first, one page.

`tier` is the resolution actually read: the dimensions have no minute
tier (a 48-hour read is hourly) and the seven-day class holds hours
only. `total` and `total_rows` cover the whole window, not the page; a
value that moved no bytes is never listed. A long-term dimension
reports `unrecorded` - device bytes in the window it has no record of
(before v1.11, a time an older panel ran, a one-table purge) - and
`window.oldest_bucket` / `window.truncated` say where its data starts.
`category` rows carry `class`: `coarse`, `unattributed` (`unknown`, no
answer) or `no_dictionary` (`""`, counted without a dictionary). `host`
and `app` answer `enabled: false` and no rows with the gate off, and
never reach back more than seven days (`window.since`, an hour key). A
single-tier read at another tier than asked fits `since`/`until` to the
tier read, so the bucket a bound falls in is kept: a minute bound on an
hourly dimension is cut to its hour, and a day `until` on the hourly
seven-day class takes every hour of that day.

`format=csv` columns: `kind,value,up,down`, plus `class` for
`dim=category`. `kind` is `value` for a dimension value and `unrecorded`
for the one row (empty `value`) carrying the device bytes the dimension
has no record of - a whole-window figure, so only on the first page
(`offset=0`). A seven-day class export with the gate off is the header
row alone.

parameters.description: The dimension: `exit` (exit node), `group` (policy group), `rule` (rule type), `category`, `country` - long-term - or `host` / `app` (hostname / app-level category id), the seven-day class, answered only with PANEL_STATS_DOMAINS on
parameters.name: dim

parameters.description: A window preset: `24h` and `48h` (minute resolution), `7d` and `30d` (hour resolution), `daily` (local-day resolution, everything held). The server computes the window from its own clock and reads it WINDOW-COMPLETE. The hour tier is written at every poll, so a minute or hour read takes its own tier alone, and a day read takes the day tier plus the hour tier, which holds the days not rolled up yet - so a 7-day total includes the newest 48 hours and `daily` includes today. A window ends at the resolution tier's retention: with the shipped retention every preset is whole, and an explicit `tier` finer than the window (e.g. `range=7d&tier=minute`) reaches back only as far as that tier holds. An explicit `tier` overrides the resolution only. Mutually exclusive with `since`/`until`, even empty ones (422). Without `range`, a read covers the single `tier` table (since v1.11 the hour table also holds the newest 48 hours).
parameters.name: range

Response Stats Chains V1 Stats Chains Get

get.description:
What share of traffic could be attributed to an app at all (#77).

DEC-6 makes this the deliverable: the per-app feature exists to enable
BLOCKING, and blocking on bad attribution takes out the wrong app on a
gateway carrying all LAN traffic. So the number comes first, and it is
measured rather than assumed.

A flow counts as attributable only when it carried a hostname (DEC-B).
Routing signals never promote one - `rule`/`rulePayload` name a
routing category, not an application, and the release gate already
refuses to read `GeoSite/cn` as proof of anything. `rules` breaks the
unattributable remainder down by the rule that routed it, which is
what distinguishes a deliberate exclusion from a real gap.

No hostname is stored to produce this: the counters are hostname-free
by construction, so the report needs none of the privacy surface the
opt-in domain table carries.

`dictionary` (#97) is a second partition of the same window: what the
category dictionary named - `app` (its app-level id kept, only with
PANEL_STATS_DOMAINS on), `coarse` (only the coarse category kept),
`unattributed` (no answer: no hostname, or one it does not know) and
`no_dictionary` (counted before v1.12, or by an older image). Each
partition sums to 100 on its own; `dictionary.total` is the bytes the
category dimension still holds per hour in the window, from
`dictionary.oldest_bucket` on.

get.description:
The newest `limit` collection gaps (1-1000). With `since`/`until`
(#98), only the gaps that overlap that window: ended at or after
`since`, started at or before `until` - compared as strings with the
stored `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ` stamps, where a shorter key names its
whole bucket on either side.

get.description:
The landing page in one read: `totals`, `timeline`, `top` lists per
dimension (the breakdown's shape), window-scoped `gaps`, `framings` at
day resolution, the `coverage` report and `invisible_traffic_hint`, all
from one read transaction, so every section describes the same moment.

Scoped to a `category` or a `host` (not both), a section the stored
tables cannot answer - the dimensions are stored independently, so a
category has no exit nodes - is `null` and `unavailable` says why;
nothing unknown is ever shown as zero. A scoped `totals` carries the
scope's `window` (where its data starts; a host's seven-day floor), a
scoped `top.device` names the scope in `within`, and `coverage` is
`null` under any scope: it is measured for the whole gateway only.
`gaps` lists the newest 100 overlapping the window, from the start of
its first bucket; `gaps_truncated` says when there may be more.

Response Stats Overview V1 Stats Overview Get

post.description:
Clears every visible stats surface (tiers, dimensions, the seven-day
tables, gap history) but preserves conn_baseline + the poll stamp -
dropping baselines would make still-open connections re-contribute
their pre-purge cumulative. An optional body narrows it to one
`device`, some `tables`, rows `before` a moment, or any combination;
no body (or `{}`) clears everything, as it always has. `rows` counts
what each table lost. The POLICY audit lives in policy.db and is
untouched - it records this purge, with its scope, like any other
mutation. A purge that touches the device tier or a dimension table
also resets the `/metrics` byte counters (#99), so purged traffic is
not served on as if it were still held.

schema.title: Response Stats Purge V1 Stats Purge Post

get.description:
The collector's own gauges (#96), one row per maintenance pass
(about a minute), kept 7 days: poll duration (ms, the mean of the last
30 polls), connections in the last snapshot, failed polls since the
panel started, seconds since the last good poll, stats.db bytes, and
mihomo's in-use memory (MiB). `null` is "not measured", never 0.
`since`/`until` compare against the minute keys (`YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM`, UTC)
as strings, like every stats read: `until=2026-10-16` ends BEFORE that
day; `until=2026-10-16T23:59` includes it.

that moved no bytes is not listed. `format=csv` (#98) exports the rows:
`bucket,up,down`, plus `bucket_tz,day_boundary` at day resolution.
